translation: ... another of the moist and cold, and a third besides these, the dry and cold, another of the dry and at the same time hot. But some of them say that there exists a mixture that is moist and at the same time cold, and another that is hot and at the same time dry, but neither the moist and at the same time hot nor the cold and at the same time dry. For it is not possible, they say, either for moisture to concur with a predominating heat or for dryness with coldness; for the moisture is consumed by the heat when it prevails, and thus the body becomes hot and at the same time dry, whereas it remains unconcocted and unelaborated in whatever bodies the heat is weak; so that it is necessary, when heat prevails, that dryness follows, and when coldness predominates, that moisture accompanies it. These men, then, have persuaded themselves on these grounds that there are in all two of the ...

... Aristotle, and likewise Theophrastus, have stated precisely what one must look to in supposing a nature to be well-tempered or ill-tempered. But these men do not even know this; rather, when they hear them saying that the animal is moist and hot, or that the mixture of the child is moist and hot, they neither understand in what sense these things are said, and they senselessly transfer the account to the seasons, as though it were the same thing, or not far different, for one's own proper mixture to be moist and hot and for that of the air surrounding us to be so. For it is not the same thing, nor is the mixture of an animal called moist and hot in the same way as the air is with a moist and hot mixture. What the cause of all these things was I shall now relate, and I shall show clearly to those willing to pay attention how small slips of those in ...

... left, there is nothing absurd. So too, then, a dog is moist and at the same time dry, and hot and at the same time cold, but not in relation to the same thing: in relation to a human it is dry, but moist as compared with an ant; and in relation to a human it is hot, but cold as compared with a lion. And indeed it is also hot as being alive, for if anything has died it is not hot; but not hot as compared with another dog, if it so happens. All these, then, are said in relation to one another by comparison; but those said as within the genus of animals are said in another manner, just as again also those according to the species of animal. For a dog, in relation to an ant and a bee, is moist, but as within the genus of animals dry; and of dogs themselves, according to species, this one is dry, that one moist, and another as ...

... of nature is judged by its activities to be in the best condition. For we say that any plant or animal whatsoever is in the best condition at that time when it performs its activities most finely. For the excellence of a fig tree is to bring to maturity the best and the most figs; in the same way, that of the vine is to bear abundantly the most and the finest clusters of grapes; that of a horse is to run most swiftly; and that of a dog is to be extremely spirited towards hunting and guarding, but most gentle towards those of its own household. All these, then, I mean both the animals and the plants, we shall say have the best and mean mixture in their own genus, not simply when there is an exact equality of the opposites, but when there exists the due proportion of it according to potency. Such a thing we say justice also is: not the equal by weight and measure, but by what is fitting ...

... for if he asked of what mixture it was as among animals, one must make the reply itself looking to the mean of all animals in mixture; but if simply and as in relation to all substance, one must then compare the opposites in it with one another and consider, no longer referring the mixture to the activities but to the bulks of the elements; but if he asked comparing it definitely with some particular thing, one must compare it with that alone. And still more, if we should be asked about one of the individual substances, as for instance Dion or this particular dog, of what sort its mixture is, one must not answer simply; for no small opportunity arises from this for the sophists to make captious misrepresentation. For if you should say that Dion is of a hot and dry mixture, it is very easy for him, putting forward some of those drier and hotter than he is, the ...

... the things of the animals and those of the plants and those of all the inanimate things, such as bronze and iron and stones and timbers, are ranged in the interval between those first ones. For none of them is either extremely hot or extremely cold or extremely moist or extremely dry, but either it is exactly in the mean between the opposites, so as to be no more hot than cold, or dry than moist, or it has inclined towards one of the extremes, so as to be more hot than cold, or more moist than dry. If, then, it should be exactly in the mean in respect of each of the two contrarieties, so as to be no more hot than cold, or dry than moist, this will be called simply well-tempered; but when one of the two has predominated, either in respect of one of the antitheses or in respect of both, it is no longer well-tempered. If then ...

... the other antithesis; the soft nerve is no longer midway between hot and cold, but falls short of heat by as much as it does of blood. So too all the other parts mentioned before are colder than skin by as much as they are also more bloodless. And the coats themselves of the most sanguineous vessels, I mean artery and vein, are bloodless and cold by nature, but they are warmed by their proximity to the blood and arrive at a mean state of mixture. The blood in its turn has its warmth from the heart; for that viscus is by nature the most sanguineous and at the same time the hottest of all the parts of the animal, and next after it the liver. But the heart falls a little short of skin in hardness, the liver by much; and accordingly it is moister than skin by as much as it is softer. And indeed also ...

... and in the movements of the limbs; and he is of good colour and always breathes easily, and is midway between sleepy and wakeful, between bare of hair and shaggy, and between black and white in colour; and he has hair, while a child, more reddish than blackish, but in his prime the reverse. And since we have also made mention of his difference according to the ages, it would be no worse now to say something about these too. I wished, then, first to go through the causes of each of the signs mentioned; but since the inquiry concerning the ages is more pressing for present purposes and renders us best equipped for the discovery of the causes, let us now take this up. Let us conceive, then, the animal just being formed in the wombs of those who bear it, so that we may know how it is moistest and hottest; for its first constitution is from ...

... the nurses of infants mould their limbs as though they were of wax; so great is the moisture in the whole body of children. But also, if you should wish either to eat a young sacrificial animal or to dissect it and examine it, you will find the flesh mucous and flabby, and the whole bony kind like freshly curdling cheese, so that the bodies of new-born animals are not even pleasant to eat because of their excessive moisture. And most of all the flesh of pigs and of sheep suffers this, because they are also especially moister, while that of goats, because it is drier, is better and more pleasant to eat. Conversely to the young animals, the aged ones have all the bones sufficiently dry and without moisture and without juice, and all their ligaments, and the flesh sinewy and hard, and the arteries and the ...

... a quantity of saliva collects in the mouth; moreover, they cough and spit up phlegm, showing then that the lung too is full of such a humour; and their stomach is filled with phlegm, and each of the joints is somewhat mucous. But none of these things contradicts the bodies of the aged being dry. For the nerves and the arteries and the veins and the membranes and the coats of all the organs you will find drier than before, but with a great deal of some phlegmatic humour or mucous moisture moulded around them both within and without. But so far are all such signs from showing old age to be moist that they even seem to me to bear witness to its dryness; for each of the parts becomes drier for this very reason, that it is no longer nourished in the same way; now through the weakness of the heat a quantity ...

... it seems to me, the pattern of the arguments being already clearly known from what we have said. For both parties reason from afar, and practically infer the prior from the posterior, and they frame their account as though the hearers already knew how growth, how concoction, how nutrition comes about; likewise they go through sensation and motion and the practical and natural activities, and they mention the genesis of sleep and the nature of foods, none of which is simple and easily known, but is in need of a very great deal of investigation, and perhaps cannot even be discovered unless one first knows how to recognize a moist and dry and hot and cold mixture. For whatever of those things they say as though already knowing it, if someone were to compel them to demonstrate it, they will in every case need the account of mixtures which is now before us; so that through one another and ...

... the present account; one must not take the proofs of them from things not yet known, but, as is right and just, what is to be taken for the demonstration ought to be either one of the evident things or one of the things previously demonstrated. Neither, then, must the genesis of sleep be mentioned, nor concoction, nor growth, nor anything else of the kind, but let the inquiry proceed from the sole and bare substance of the underlying things, just as we did in the first book also. For having distinguished that what is in actuality is one thing and what is in potentiality another, we said that one must first give an account of what is already in actuality hot and cold and dry and moist, and then in this way proceed to what is so in potentiality. Ready to hand for all and known is the [recognition] of things already hot in actuality ...

... positing principles and elements, to have strayed so far from the men who posited these as not to know both that the starting points of every demonstration are the things evident to sense and to intellect, and that whoever is at a loss about these seeks in vain about the rest, not having left himself even a point from which to begin. Whence, then, they turned to so long a wandering and attempted to seek by reason the diagnosis of perceptible things, I cannot even conceive. And for this reason I judge by touch what is hot in actuality; but if something is not yet hot but is fit to become such, which indeed is also named hot in potentiality, this I try to discover by reason. With them, I know not how, everything has been turned upside down, and a long rhetoric has been practised about the arguments. Let us, then, leave these men, having reminded ourselves at least this much now too, that ...

... nor is it reasonable at all to confirm the prior from the posterior. Let us judge, then, by sensation the hot and the cold body, that which is already such in actuality and no longer in potentiality, setting aside the first judgement and all the other signs. And you, as one who will judge well, I release to the trial; but I myself shall set out my own judgement. For, touching many bodies in succession carefully, not only of children or infants but also of adolescents and of men in their prime, I found that neither party speaks the truth, neither those who said simply that the man in his prime is hotter than the child nor those who said he is colder. For if, removing all the other alterations from outside, you consider the differences arising from age alone, neither will appear to you simply hotter; for their heats differ in quality, with unequal transpiration, on account of which also ...

... the spinal marrow by kind, but all the other marrows are of a different nature. The brain is moister and hotter than the spinal marrow, and for this reason also softer; and indeed of the brain itself the front parts are moister by as much as they are also softer. All these, however, are not only moister than skin but also colder; and in general everything bloodless is colder than the sanguineous. Nearest to skin is also the nature of the soft nerves, while that of the hard ones is just like skin itself, in respect of moisture and dryness, that is; for in heat it falls short by as much as the wholly bloodless can be expected to fall short of a sanguineous body. The flesh of the spleen and of the kidneys and of the liver is moister than skin by as much as it is also softer, and hotter by as much as it is also richer in blood. And indeed the flesh of the heart ...

... and catarrhs and coughs and coryzas and a quantity of saliva; for all these show him to be colder and moister, and still more so if he falls into such conditions on chance occasions. Baldness, on the other hand, follows upon dryness, and the growth of black and abundant hair is a sign of good mixture of the brain. In this way, then, one must always consider the mixture, examining each part individually, and not dare to pronounce about all from one, as some have done, saying that the snub-nosed are moist and the hook-nosed dry, and those whose eyes are small dry, those whose eyes are large moist. And on this point they have indeed disagreed among themselves; for some, supposing the eyes to be among the moist parts, in whomever they find them larger, [assert] moistness of mixture in ...

... the same, or to evacuate the moisture of something scattered in certain spaces, or to render its proper mixture drier. For an uneven dyscrasia arises in inflamed parts, the homoeomerous bodies not yet having departed from their proper nature but still being changed and altered, while all the spaces between are filled with the flux. All things, then, that are hot and moist in mixture, when applied to those so disposed, evacuate that superfluity which has occupied the spaces between the homoeomerous bodies, but are so far from drying the bodies themselves that they even impart moisture to them. That, then, is how the truth stands; but what has been said needs demonstration, which, thinking it too long to be added in this treatise, and moreover in need of a hearer versed in the power of drugs, I defer; at least ...

... or, if you like, the yellow bile, and that all the others are hot by accident through partaking of these, will it not be necessary that the animal becomes hotter in two ways, either by acquiring more hot humours or by having them hotter than before? To me it certainly seems so. And in the same way, I think, it will also become colder in two ways, either by more of the cold humours being bred, such as phlegm and black bile, or by the quality alone being changed while the due proportion of all of them remains. What wonder, then, that as long as a food cold by nature, such as purslane and lettuce, is being concocted, the body is filled with cold quality, but when they have been thoroughly concocted and have become good blood, the body becomes in turn hotter than itself through the generation of the hot humour? And indeed ...

... condition, if it is simple and single; but the judgement by time is determined as follows: what appears evidently to cool or heat at the same moment as it is applied would surely be such in itself and through itself; but what does so in time might perhaps be brought to this from some accident, as in tetanus, in midsummer, in a well-fleshed young man, an affusion of much cold water produces a recall of heat. But that cold water does not heat in itself is clear from the first impact; for it produces a sensation of cooling. And indeed it also cools the skin as long as it is being poured upon it, and it furnishes the warmth neither in all bodies nor during the affusion, but only in well-fleshed young men in the middle of summer, after they have stopped pouring. Just as, then, in those whom it strikes ...

... of the ease of bearing and the benefit, this is of necessity cold, [even if] in other cases it sometimes appears hot; for in those cases, examined precisely, it will be found heating not in itself but by some accident. And when we say 'in itself', or 'primarily', or 'through nothing intermediate', the same thing is signified by all the expressions in their force; and the exercise in all these together, with their proper examples, we shall carry out in the commentaries on drugs. Now, having again recalled what I said already before, I shall try to put the fitting conclusion to the present treatise. Since the hot body was said in many ways, both that which has the extreme quality, the element itself, and that named according to its predominance, and further that said in relation to another, either in relation to the symmetrical of the same kind or in relation to anything whatever ...

... and also with rose cerate it helps greatly; for which, indeed, and for such conditions many other drugs will be mentioned in the following book, some having a power similar to the phoenicine, some even more active. But for rheumatic affections this drug is the best of all, and has often accomplished something greater than hope. When, then, once a thigh had suppurated near the groin, while the inflammation throughout it was unconcocted, the leg was positioned by us so that the ichors flowed out towards the groin; but at the ulcer that had formed, this happening over a longer time, the flux that had settled into the thigh was evacuated, but a fistulous condition arose under the skin throughout the whole thigh, so that [we] wished to incise it near the kneecap, in order that there might be an outflow on both sides for the ichors ...

... having taken vinegar in addition; for that one is useful at every time. But the white [plaster] made with pepper is useful for burns that have been flayed, when they are being brought to a scar; before that, by itself it is useless, but dissolved in myrtle oil it is useful, not however with equal strength to the drugs properly suited to burns from fire. Heras says that it is also suitable for those who have been bitten; but here too there is need of a distinction: for in hard and hard-to-concoct [cases] the drug is weaker, but in more moderate ones sufficient, and especially in old men and children and women, and, to speak summarily, in the soft-fleshed. The drug is also useful for ionthi, as Heras also wrote truly; but he pronounced without distinction about the exanthemata; for of these too it heals those that are moderately hardish, but the ...

... but the measure is not equal to the Roman; for they use, one one sextarius measure, another another. Among the Romans, at any rate, the sextarius holds one litra and a half and a sixth, so that the ounces are twenty in all, which they mostly measure with horns scored on the outside with certain circular lines. But some have falsely supposed that the Roman sextarius holds eighteen measured ounces. It seems, then, that Heras too, when he writes kotyle, means half of the sextarius; and they indicate either the nine ounces of the litra-horn or the ten; for this is unclear. But whether the drug is also suitable for those bitten by rabid dogs, whether swallowed or applied externally, it is not possible to know by reasoning; for it has been shown by us that such drugs have their activity by the whole peculiarity of their substance ...

... concerning food, how the bad and the not bad are said as among relatives, and of course the harmful and the beneficial. For in another sense you might say that the Attalic is better than this plaster, in that it is of more uses. Indeed Asclepiades himself, writing next after this one now mentioned that very [plaster] made with white pepper, does not name it Attalic but Pamphilian, not knowing, I think, the man who first discovered it, but adding the name of the one who used it and gave it to him. Its promise, then, he wrote word for word as follows: 'Another, called Pamphilian, a successful drug; it acts on old and intractable [lesions], carbuncles, epinyctides, achores, psoric conditions; it glues together sinuses; it acts on abscesses, condylomata; and it is almost a drug of more uses.' He says that it is composed of white lead ...

... let each of these be precisely, for the sake of contributing something to the whiteness of the drug. And about the white lead too it has been said before, and about the oil, and the manner of boiling, and the surrounding air, and the fire, how each of them may contribute something to the whiteness. And just as in the other cases, so also in these one must, knowing the powers of water and vinegar and sea water and of the whitest wine, mix in the composition what is most useful for the condition being treated. For in callous ulcers which have thick and hard lips and need much thinning, those ground in vinegar and sea water are more useful than those ground in water; but in those in which the fluid discharged in the ulcers is acrid and biting, one must rather have them ground in water ...

... each of the metallic [ingredients]; just as, again, rather in wine, in those where the fluid flowing onto the ulcers appears abundant. Each of these, then, which I have mentioned, ground in each of the liquids mentioned over several days, I put in each time into the drugs made with white lead and litharge, and I found by trial that all of them cicatrize very finely; and some recipes I also gave to friends in need of such drugs, by whom too, when brought to trial, they were seen to preserve their promise. When, then, the litharge has been boiled beforehand with the white lead, as has been said, and the drug has come near to a non-staining consistency, one must add larch or terebinth resin with white wax, and when these have been well united, add the metallic [ingredients], having the following proportion: of the litharge and the white lead, as usual, a litra of each, let it be boiled with two litrae of oil, often ...

... but if some scirrhous part of its inflammation should remain, one must apply one of the sufficiently drying [drugs]. Since, then, something appeared to be lacking, I first used the drug made with the root of dragon arum, which has everything else the same as the Egyptian drug called the Isis, but has taken in addition the root of dragon arum; and next after this, having used the one called the Athena, from that I passed finally to the cicatrizing [drugs]. In another case, smearing the bared parts of the wound with the pastille dissolved in boiled-down must, I put on from outside the euphorbium, having mixed it with wax and resin in such quantity that it became at the same time plaster-like and preserved the power of the euphorbium. How one might compose the drug looking to these aims I shall say next; for indeed I also made another drug with vinegar ...

... just as with resin and pitch; for this reason I mix resin or pitch or a part of each with the cerate. It is clear, then, that when these are mixed in, the oil must no longer be put in equal to them; for wax needs much fat for moisture, but of the resins the wholly dry need little, while the moist even want to take in some dry substance in addition for a plaster-like consistency. Among the waxes, then, the difference in respect of moisture and dryness is not great, but in the resins, conversely, as also in pitch, the difference of the dry ones from the moist is very great. The driest of the resins, then, is the one which some call roasted, others colophony; second is the one from the pottery-works, unpurified and unroasted; but if one purifies it ...

... in the work; some of those inexperienced in anatomy, confusing the same thing, flay off from all the muscles the underlying membranes, not knowing that these are sewn together with the muscles without danger, but most dangerously the tendons that are flattened similarly to them; but however much they are flattened, they are nevertheless still thicker than the membranes and harder. You will see sufficiently thin tendons also in all the muscles of the abdominal wall except the two straight ones, upon which the membranous aponeuroses of the oblique ones are laid. But no other tendon besides those mentioned is flattened in a membranous way; for all those that are flattened preserve a sufficient thickness, so as to escape no one's notice. The sympathy of the overlying parts as far as the origin of the nerves itself is no less in the muscles at the end of the thigh and in those inserting into the elbow of the forearm and ...

... you have seen me doing continually, not with this alone but also with the ammoniac incense. There is also the drug written after this by the Tarentine, of the same promise, in the following proportion: chalcitis 25 dr., cadmia 12 dr.; having ground them separately and mixed them, pour on unadulterated wine, having boiled it, so that it is kneaded moderately; then grind until it is dried; and having melted wax 50 dr., terebinth resin 30 dr., myrtle [oil] 8 kot., mix into the cerate of the dry ingredients 20 dr. This drug too has nothing of the emollient; but in the mixing with the cerate, the one trained rationally in the methods I set out would suitably produce the fitting quantity of the mixture for each of the ulcers. And rightly also the unadulterated wine, that is, that with which sea water has not been mixed ...

... the meltable [ingredients], having let them cool somewhat, sprinkle the dry ones over them, stirring carefully. One must have ready, ground with vinegar, myrrh, frankincense, bdellium, opopanax; and into these the contents of the pan are put, and they are ground so that lumps do not form. When it is in good condition, take it up into a wooden box, having smeared it first with iris oil. On the third kind of hard-to-treat ulcers, about which Asclepiades wrote this word for word: 'In ulcers that do not close at all, or that close but break open again, either the flesh being corrupted or the underlying bones too being decayed, one must use the preparations set out below. For chironian and intractable [ulcers], a successful drug: copper scale, scraped verdigris, 1 oz. each; wax half a litra; larch resin 1 1/2 oz.; [pour] the meltable ones over the dry, and taking it up, use it, softening it carefully and throwing on a small flat dressing over ...'

... the metallic [ingredients] with vinegar, and after these adding the dry ones and grinding again; then, when these have a muddy consistency, mixing in the meltable ones, as has been said before. Another: bitumen and terebinth resin and Bruttian pitch, 1 litra each; oil 24 dr.; litharge and white lead and manna and verdigris and scale and opopanax, of each equal to the twenty-four drachmas of the oil; ladanum two oz., which is 16 dr.; and two kotylai of vinegar. This drug too is prepared similarly to the two before it. Another: chrysocolla and scale and stomoma, 4 dr. each; verdigris and chalcanthum, of each half, that is 2 dr. each; wax 25 dr., that is 3 oz. and one drachma; terebinth resin 2 oz., that is 16 dr. Melt the wax with the terebinth ...

... it checks haemorrhoids, and it acts extremely well in [affections] about the bladder. It contains: frankincense 4 dr., myrrh 4 dr., saffron 4 dr., Illyrian iris 4 dr., bdellium 4 dr., scale 12 dr., chalcanthum 4 dr., split alum 4 dr., round [alum] 4 dr., ammoniac incense 4 dr., misy 4 dr., rinds of sweet pomegranate 4 dr., aristolochia, oak-gall, omphacitis, 8 dr. each (otherwise 16), chalcitis 4 dr., ammoniac incense 4 dr., oak mistletoe 8 dr., opopanax 8 dr., scraped verdigris 8 dr., acacia 8 dr., flower of roses 8 dr., terebinth 1 mina (others 50 dr.), poppy juice 6 dr., wax 2 minae (others 4 dr.), suet of a calf, treated, 1 mina (others 150), common vinegar 2 kotylai, wine for these dry [ingredients] ...

Of verdigris and of Indian aloe, and of burnt copper and good diphryges, sixteen and a half of each component; twenty drachmas of galbanum and four; of manna and of frankincense the equal, twice twelve; of ammoniac twice five and twice twenty; sixteen drachmas of Attic propolis; of long aristolochia twice ten drachmas; twice six drachmas of the scale of Cyprian copper; and of the driest gentian root the equal. To all these add of the herb dittany, dry, having its flower, twenty holkai. Putting litharge, ground fine, with oil into a new earthenware pan with a wide mouth, boil on a light and gentle fire, stirring with a spatula, until it comes to the thickness of Attic honey. And adding again the equal of the scale, boil more fiercely; then, when the drug has become tawny, add the copper and the diphryges, making the drug non-staining and set; add the wax and the ...

... and of iris instead of the molybdaena; put in two parts of litharge, and of the rest one part each. A dry septic, of Lecanius Areius: arsenic 1 litra, quicklime 2 dr.; grind in water for 30 days, changing the water twice a day, in the sun; then, having dried it, use it. A sitz-bath for haemorrhoids, that of Phanias: chalcanthum, split alum, chalcitis, raw misy, sandarach, 4 dr. each; keep everything ground fine; at the time of use, old pickled urine of one man, 2 sextarii by measure; put it into an earthenware basin, and of the drug 12 dr.; keep pouring in more of the urine, so that the two sextarii are always maintained. Use this, seating [the patient] in it, for 7 days; for in these it acts. When it becomes glutinous, smear the anus round with the sediment. A dry [powder] cicatrizing flesh, non-biting, as Harpocras: sandarach, chrysocolla, arsenic, the equal of each ...

... of wax, having neither of these, but the ammoniac incense alone, when put in, will make the drug parched. But for plaster-making (for it is no worse to name it so) both the wax and the resin are useful; for the softening and dispersing belong to the drug from the ammoniac alone, which is foremost among the emollients and also a rival to the discutients. Having recalled what was said in the fifth [book] of the On the Powers of Simple Drugs, of what sort the mixture must be in such drugs, you will need no further new instruction. For the first powers, which are active in drugs, are in heat and coldness and moisture and dryness; the second are the emollient and the discutient and the repellent and the attractive and the concoctive and the detergent and the septic, just as also ...

... of all carefully, again strain off a little; if you see it of good colour and well blended, lift the pot at once from the fire, and add galbanum softened beforehand. But if the drug is much harder, add oil to it for a good blend. Thus straining it then into another vessel, knead it cold with the hands and so store it away. Another I shall subjoin, of the same kind as the one before this. It acts on the affections which I mentioned before; this one cicatrizes better than all drugs ulcers that are intractable and callous and chronic; the exanthemata arising on the face this one heals without any bad biting; and seats that have fissures and hardnesses, the condylomatous ones, and it removes calluses. Prepare it thus: a mina of good litharge (a mina is a litra and a third part of a litra); of good Pontic wax half a mina; of verdigris a fourth part of a mina, good, scraped ...

... scrofulous swellings; repressing every oedema, and healing the watery conditions of liver or spleen; bringing on copious excretions of urine; it also resolves chronic sciaticas. Using this, Ulpianus, a gifted young man, helped very many. It contains a litra of Pontic wax, one; and one of the roasted [resin] and one of the pine [resin]; of fresh quicklime 1 ounce; of split alum 1 ounce; and equal to one of these of the Pontic arsenic. Pouring a little fragrant vinegar on these, grind sufficiently in a larger mortar. Adding a little oil to the wax and resin, melting it over a fire of fierce flame, and mixing all carefully, and making malagmas, making it of the thickness of a non-staining [drug], keep it stored. Use it where needed with a fresh pad. And Kratistos, the father of the drug, said that also for the riddance of long diseases ...

... which also heal small inflammations. Of the compound emollients some are, as one might say, weaker, in the first order; some not much stronger than these, in the second; and some others in the third, and besides these still others in the fourth. One should use, as has been said before, for slight hardnesses and soft bodies those of the first order, but for bodies and affections stronger than these those of the second, just as also those of the third and of the fourth proportionally. They also set out those belonging to each of them individually. Emollient drugs of the first order: butter, or the Colophonian resin, and white wax, not old, equal by weight, the three melted together, are emollients of the first order; and so is the parygros, when it is fresh.

This Menecrates did because it often happens that errors are made in the writings not only by people unwillingly but also by some willingly, out of envy, some making the letter o into theta by drawing another transverse line through the middle of the round line, and the letter iota [into another] by likewise adding another transverse line; just as also, when one line is scraped off from the letter rho, it happens that the character of iota is left. In the same way, from many letters, by the addition of some, by the composition of others, by the removal of others, it happens that the alteration of the characters indicating them comes about. But Menecrates achieved nothing more for the time following, since those copying his book did not write the names of the numbers in full letters but by means of the characters indicating them.
